passage:
The history of jazz piano is in many respects a history of productive misreadings. Each generation of pianists has inherited the innovations of its predecessors and then, through selective emphasis and willful distortion, transformed them into something new. Nowhere is this process more visible than in the transition from the stride tradition of the 1920s to the bebop revolution of the 1940s — a transition that standard jazz historiography tends to describe as an abrupt rupture, but that on closer examination reveals itself as a deeply ambivalent inheritance.

Stride piano, as practiced by James P. Johnson, Fats Waller, and their contemporaries, was built on a particular tension: the left hand alternated between bass notes on the beat and midrange chords on the offbeat, producing a rocking momentum that anchored dancers to the floor, while the right hand was free to pursue melodic flights of considerable sophistication. Critics have often treated stride primarily as entertainment music — crowd-pleasing, physically engaging, and technically demanding but ultimately decorative. This reading is not false, but it is incomplete. Stride pianists were simultaneously theorizing about rhythm: the alternating left hand was not merely a groove machine but an argument about the relationship between pulse and accent, between the predictable and the surprising. What appeared on the surface as a formula for crowd satisfaction was, beneath that surface, a rigorous investigation of rhythmic counterpoint.

The bebop pianists who came of age in the 1940s — Bud Powell foremost among them — are typically seen as breaking decisively with this tradition. And in one sense they did: Powell stripped away the striding left hand almost entirely, replacing it with sparse, unpredictable chord clusters that refused to anchor the listener in any comfortable groove. But the received narrative of rupture obscures a deeper continuity. Powell's liberation of the left hand was not an abandonment of stride's rhythmic investigation; it was, rather, its logical extension. Where stride pianists had staged a dialogue between regularity and surprise within a metrically stable framework, Powell collapsed that framework itself, pushing the implicit tension in stride piano toward a limit the stride masters had approached but never crossed. The bebop left hand does not ignore the questions that stride posed; it answers them by dissolving the terms of the question entirely.

To acknowledge this continuity is not to flatten the real differences between the two traditions. Stride was communal and kinetic, designed for bodies in motion; bebop was cerebral and confrontational, designed, in Thelonious Monk's famous formulation, for listeners who would sit down and listen. Yet even this contrast conceals a shared ambition: both traditions sought to make explicit the latent complexity of rhythm that popular dance music had always exploited but never theorized. What separates stride and bebop is less a matter of musical philosophy than of audience and occasion — a shift in social context that transformed the same underlying inquiry into two apparently opposite artistic programs.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stride piano was a more intellectually sophisticated tradition than jazz critics have generally acknowledged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bud Powell's bebop innovations represented a complete and deliberate rejection of the stride piano tradition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although stride and bebop piano appear sharply opposed, they share a deeper continuity rooted in a common rhythmic inquiry, and their differences are better explained by social context than by musical philosophy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jazz historiography has systematically underestimated the influence of James P. Johnson and Fats Waller on subsequent generations of pianists.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The transition from stride to bebop illustrates the general principle that artistic movements always build on the traditions they appear to overthrow.

explanations.correct: The passage argues two interlocking claims: that the stride-to-bebop transition conceals a deep continuity (the same rhythmic inquiry extended to its limit), and that the real differences between the traditions are matters of social context rather than musical philosophy. C integrates both strands across all four paragraphs.
explanations.A: Too narrow — this captures only part of paragraph 2's argument and ignores the continuity claim that is the passage's central thesis.
explanations.B: This is the 'received narrative of rupture' that the passage explicitly contests; it is the view the author argues against, not the main point.
explanations.D: The passage mentions these pianists but does not make a claim about historiography's treatment of their influence specifically; this is a plausible-world detail that overstates a subordinate point.
explanations.E: Too broad — the passage argues for a specific mechanism of continuity in jazz, not a universal principle about all artistic movements. Generalizing beyond the passage's scope is a classic over-broad trap.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard jazz historiography's account of the stride-to-bebop transition can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissive, because it fails to recognize any connection between the two traditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautiously approving, because it correctly identifies the technical demands of both traditions

choices.label: C
choices.text: partially accepting but ultimately critical, because it captures a surface truth while missing the deeper continuity

choices.label: D
choices.text: deeply skeptical of its descriptions of stride piano but fully accepting of its characterization of bebop

choices.label: E
choices.text: sympathetic, because the social differences between the two traditions do justify treating them as a rupture

explanations.correct: The author does not dismiss the standard account outright — the passage concedes that 'in one sense' the beboppers did break with stride — but argues that the rupture narrative obscures a deeper continuity. C captures this nuanced, partially-accepting-but-ultimately-critical stance precisely.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author does not dismiss the standard account as entirely wrong, only as incomplete, mirroring the same move made about stride critics in paragraph 2.
explanations.B: The author is not approving of the standard account; the passage frames the historiographical consensus as the target of correction.
explanations.D: The author does not split admiration/skepticism this way; the critique of the standard account applies to its overall narrative of rupture, not differentially to each tradition.
explanations.E: The author explicitly states that the social contrast 'conceals a shared ambition' — so social differences do not, in the author's view, justify the rupture narrative.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A general claim about jazz history is introduced; the stride tradition is described and its standard interpretation corrected; the bebop tradition is described and its standard interpretation corrected; a synthesis reconciles the two traditions while acknowledging their real differences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing theories of jazz history are introduced; evidence for each is presented in turn; the author concludes that neither theory is adequate and proposes a third.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biographical account of Bud Powell's innovations is presented; these innovations are contrasted with stride piano; the contrast is then used to argue for a new theory of musical influence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stride tradition is described in technical detail; bebop is then described as its direct descendant; the passage concludes by urging a revision of jazz curricula.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A claim about artistic misreading is introduced; two case studies illustrating the claim are examined; the passage ends by noting exceptions to the general principle.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the general claim about productive misreadings and the stride-to-bebop transition. Paragraph 2 describes stride and corrects the entertainment-only reading. Paragraph 3 describes bebop and corrects the rupture narrative. Paragraph 4 synthesizes: real differences acknowledged, shared ambition identified, social context as the true separator. A maps onto all four paragraphs accurately.
explanations.B: The passage does not present two competing theories and then reject both in favor of a third; it presents one standard narrative and corrects it.
explanations.C: The passage is not biographical and does not focus on Powell alone; Powell is introduced as an example in paragraph 3, not as the primary subject.
explanations.D: The passage does not describe bebop as stride's 'direct descendant' in a simple lineage sense, and it makes no argument about jazz curricula — a plausible-but-unused move trap.
explanations.E: The passage does not present two distinct case studies, nor does it note exceptions to its principle at the end.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, stride piano's left hand technique was characterized by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: sparse, unpredictable chord clusters that refused to establish a groove

choices.label: B
choices.text: a continuous melodic line that competed with the right hand for rhythmic primacy

choices.label: C
choices.text: an alternation between bass notes on the beat and midrange chords on the offbeat

choices.label: D
choices.text: a metrically free accompaniment designed to liberate the right hand from rhythmic constraint

choices.label: E
choices.text: a rocking pattern derived directly from West African drumming traditions

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that 'the left hand alternated between bass notes on the beat and midrange chords on the offbeat.' C is a direct paraphrase of this detail.
explanations.A: This describes Powell's bebop left hand technique (paragraph 3), not stride — a wrong-sentence trap.
explanations.B: The passage describes the right hand as pursuing melodic flights, not the left; attributing a continuous melodic line to the left hand inverts the passage's description.
explanations.D: Stride's left hand was metrically stable, not free; 'metrically free' is a description that applies to bebop's departure from stride.
explanations.E: The passage makes no mention of West African drumming traditions; this is a plausible world-fact that the passage does not state.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about Bud Powell's bebop style?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It was motivated primarily by a desire to make jazz inaccessible to general audiences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extended the rhythmic investigation implicit in stride piano by pushing that investigation past the boundaries stride had maintained.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It represented a complete departure from all prior jazz piano traditions, including stride.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It answered the questions posed by stride piano by restoring a more stable metric framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It was primarily significant for having introduced chord clusters as a substitute for single-note melody lines.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that Powell's liberation of the left hand 'was not an abandonment of stride's rhythmic investigation; it was, rather, its logical extension,' and that Powell pushed 'the implicit tension in stride piano toward a limit the stride masters had approached but never crossed.' B closely paraphrases this inference.
explanations.A: The passage does not attribute Powell's motivations to a desire for inaccessibility; it situates bebop's cerebral quality within a social context shift, not intentional exclusion.
explanations.C: This is precisely the 'received narrative of rupture' the author contests; attributing it to the author inverts the passage's argument.
explanations.D: The passage states the opposite: Powell 'collapsed' the stable metric framework rather than restoring one.
explanations.E: The passage mentions chord clusters as a feature of Powell's style but does not present this as his primary significance; this is a too-narrow plausible detail.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely refers to Thelonious Monk's formulation that bebop was designed 'for listeners who would sit down and listen' primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that bebop pianists were contemptuous of audiences who preferred stride piano

choices.label: B
choices.text: support the claim that bebop's cerebral quality represented a philosophical break from jazz's dance origins

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide a concrete example of the social and contextual differences between stride and bebop, while framing those differences as surface-level rather than philosophical

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that Monk, not Powell, was the central theorist of the bebop piano tradition

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that bebop audiences were more musically educated than the dancers who attended stride performances

explanations.correct: The Monk quotation appears in paragraph 4 to characterize bebop as 'cerebral and confrontational, designed for listeners who would sit down and listen,' in direct contrast to stride's kinetic, communal quality. But the surrounding argument immediately qualifies this contrast as concealing a 'shared ambition.' The quotation thus illustrates the real (but surface-level) social difference while the passage frames it as secondary to the underlying philosophical continuity. C captures both the illustrative and the qualifying functions.
explanations.A: The passage does not attribute contempt for stride audiences to bebop pianists; this overstates the contrast and attributes an attitude not present in the text.
explanations.B: This partially captures the quotation's role but misses the passage's point that the contrast is a matter of audience and occasion, not musical philosophy — the passage explicitly says 'less a matter of musical philosophy.'
explanations.D: The passage does not argue for Monk's centrality over Powell's; the quotation is used for its content, not to establish a hierarchy of theorists.
explanations.E: The passage makes no comparative claim about the musical education of audiences in either tradition; this is a plausible-world inference not licensed by the text.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's central claim about the relationship between stride and bebop piano?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Archival recordings show that Bud Powell attended live stride performances throughout the late 1930s and frequently discussed rhythmic counterpoint with stride musicians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Musicological analysis reveals that bebop's tempos were, on average, significantly faster than those of stride performances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several prominent stride pianists publicly criticized bebop as unnecessarily complex and incomprehensible to general audiences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jazz scholars have documented that the dance halls where stride was performed had declined sharply in number by the early 1940s.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcriptions of Powell's compositions show that his left-hand chord voicings frequently implied the metric positions that stride's alternating bass pattern had made explicit.

explanations.correct: The author's central claim is that bebop was not a rupture but an extension of stride's rhythmic investigation — specifically that Powell's left hand answered, rather than abandoned, stride's questions about pulse and accent. If Powell's chord voicings implicitly retained the metric positions that stride had made explicit, this directly supports the continuity thesis by showing that bebop preserved stride's rhythmic framework in a transformed, implicit form.
explanations.A: Powell's biographical exposure to stride would support a general influence claim, but not the specific musical-structural claim about rhythmic investigation; this is relevant but does not directly address the passage's argument about how the left hand functions.
explanations.B: Tempo differences would highlight a difference between the traditions, not the underlying continuity — this is more consistent with the rupture narrative the author contests.
explanations.C: Stride pianists criticizing bebop would support the narrative of rupture and conflict, not the author's continuity thesis; this choice slightly weakens rather than strengthens the central claim.
explanations.D: The decline of dance halls supports the social-context explanation for the shift in bebop's audience (paragraph 4), but this is a secondary point about occasion, not the primary claim about shared rhythmic philosophy.
